subject: botany
question_text: Give a brief account of dinoflagellates.

verification.note: Sourced from the Junior Fastrack botany book, Biological Classification chapter (book pp.4-5), which prints the question and a model answer but NO star ranks and NO year citations. Only ONE source book is held for botany — the TSBIE Basic Learning Material in hand covers physics only, and no botany board paper is in the corpus — so the two-book union check and the past-paper back-test are both STRUCTURALLY IMPOSSIBLE for this card, not merely pending: 'not checked' must never be read as 'checked and clean'. The mark split is a claim until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. The book prints 'Red tides of mediterranean sea is due to inhabitation of Gonyaulax' — 'inhabitation' is a scan garble; the standard cause is the rapid multiplication of Gonyaulax, which this card states.

steps.label: Habitat and cell wall
lines: They appear yellow, green, brown, blue or
red depending on the main pigments.
The cell wall has stiff cellulose plates
steps.why: Habitat, pigments and the plated cellulose wall identify the group before its movement and special members are described.
common_mistakes: Writing silica walls here. Silica belongs to diatoms; dinoflagellates have cellulose plates.
Writing fresh water as the main habitat. They are mostly marine.
steps.memory_tip: Marine cells in cellulose plates, coloured by their pigments.
steps.margin_note: Three one-line facts open the account.

steps.label: Flagella
lines: There are two flagella: one lies
in a furrow between the wall plates.
steps.why: The two flagella set at right angles make the cell spin as it swims; the common name whirling whips describes exactly this movement.
common_mistakes: Writing both flagella as longitudinal. One longitudinal plus one transverse in the furrow is the tested arrangement.
steps.memory_tip: One along, one across — the across one sits in the furrow.
steps.margin_note: The arrangement of the two flagella is the marked detail.

steps.label: Nucleus and special members
lines: The nucleus is called a mesokaryon.
steps.why: The mesokaryon — a nucleus with condensed chromosomes even between divisions — and the light-emitting Noctiluca are the two special facts expected in a brief account.
common_mistakes: Writing mesosome for mesokaryon. A mesosome is a bacterial membrane structure.
Attaching bioluminescence to Gonyaulax. The light emitter is Noctiluca.
steps.memory_tip: Meso-karyon for the nucleus; Nocti-luca, Latin for night light, for bioluminescence.

steps.label: Red tides
lines: rapidly that the sea appears red — red tides.
The toxins released kill fish and other

lines.text: Plates, two flagella, mesokaryon, red tides.

steps.why: The red tide closes the account with the group's most examined fact: rapid multiplication of Gonyaulax colours the sea, and the released toxins kill fish. (The book prints 'due to inhabitation of Gonyaulax' — a scan garble for rapid multiplication.)
common_mistakes: Writing that the red colour itself kills the fish. The killer is the released toxins.
Naming cyanobacteria here. Red tides in this chapter are by the dinoflagellate Gonyaulax.
steps.memory_tip: Gonyaulax multiplies, the sea reddens, the toxins kill fish — three facts in order.
steps.margin_note: End with the red tide pair: cause (multiplication) and harm (toxins).

insider_note: A brief account is marked as four separate facts; the mesokaryon and the furrow arrangement of the flagella separate full marks from three.
